c.install_help_windows:
No C compiler found.

Pick whichever is easiest for you:

  1. w64devkit  -- a single portable zip, no installer, ~80 MB.
     https://github.com/skeeto/w64devkit/releases
     Unzip it, then add its bin\ folder to PATH (or just relaunch this
     app -- C:\w64devkit\bin is auto-detected).

  2. MSYS2      -- full package manager, best long term.
     https://www.msys2.org  then:  pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc

  3. Visual Studio -- you already have VS installed, but without the C++
     toolset. Open the Visual Studio Installer, click Modify, and tick
     'Desktop development with C++'.

Re-check from the Tools menu once installed -- no restart needed.

java.install_help_windows:
No JDK found.

Pick whichever is easiest for you:

  1. Adoptium (Eclipse Temurin) -- a standard, free JDK installer.
     https://adoptium.net

  2. winget      -- from an elevated prompt:
     winget install EclipseAdoptium.Temurin.21.JDK

  3. Visual Studio -- if it is already installed, open the Visual
     Studio Installer, click Modify, and tick 'Java development'.

Re-check from the Tools menu once installed -- no restart needed.
Make sure 'javac', not just 'java', ends up on PATH -- some installs
(and some Linux package managers) offer a JRE-only package that runs
programs but cannot compile one.

  Debian/Ubuntu:  sudo apt install default-jdk
  Fedora:         sudo dnf install java-latest-openjdk-devel
  macOS:          brew install openjdk

No assembler found.

exit.access_violation: access violation (a bad address in a mov, or a pointer argument followed past the end of what it points at)
exit.divide_by_zero: integer division by zero (idiv by a zero divisor)
exit.integer_overflow: the quotient did not fit in the destination register -- idiv faults rather than wrapping (was rdx sign-extended with cdq or cqo first?)
exit.illegal_instruction: illegal instruction (did execution run off the end of a procedure without a ret?)
exit.stack_overflow: stack overflow (runaway recursion, or a push with no matching pop inside a loop?)

dialog.authoring_help_message:
A problem is one JSON file under:
{root}

Required fields:
  title, language, statement, harness, tests,
  and reference_solution (or reference_solution_b64)

The harness supplies main(); the candidate supplies the function.
Each test is {{name, stdin, expected_stdout, description}}.

Every reference solution is run against the full suite before the
problem is offered -- a problem whose reference fails is disabled.

Optional 'generator' adds randomised cases:
  {{"count": 4, "source": "def generate(rng, count): ..."}}
It returns inputs only -- {{name, stdin, description}} -- and the
expected output is captured from the reference solution, so the
two can never disagree. Ctrl+R draws a new data set.

See README.md for the full schema and a worked example.

dialog.show_solution_hint_nudge: The hint (F1) gives you the idea without the code.
dialog.guides_help_message:
Pages that open in your browser rather than in the app:

  Diagram          the problem's specification, drawn. Only the
                   problems whose spec IS a diagram have one
  Hint             the idea, the traps, and the cases to think
                   about -- no answer in it
  Worked solution  the whole answer, a trace of it running, and
                   the wrong turns worth recognising

They live beside the problem file and are found by name:

  c_sum_array.json
  c_sum_array.hint.html
  c_sum_array.solution.html

There is nothing to register -- drop the files next to the JSON
and this menu picks them up. They share problems/guides.css.

A diagram page renders its Mermaid source with a script fetched
from a CDN. With no network it shows the source instead, which
is the same specification in text -- and that text is in the
problem statement too, so the app never needs the network.

'python -m crucible --guides' lists which problems are missing
a hint or a worked solution.
